questions.prompt: Why can a negative-feedback loop whose loop gain has only ONE pole never become unstable?
options: Because a single pole has no gain
A single pole contributes at most \(-90^\circ\) of phase, so \(T\) can never reach \(-180^\circ\) (i.e. \(T=-1\))
Because a single pole makes the loop gain grow with frequency
Because single-pole loops have no feedback
questions.explanation: \(\angle\dfrac{T_0}{1+j\omega\tau}=-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)\to-90^\circ\) at most. The feedback never turns positive, so there is always at least \(90^\circ\) of phase margin.

questions.prompt: A feedback system oscillates at a frequency \(\omega_x\) when
options: \(T(j\omega_x)=-1\): unity magnitude with \(-180^\circ\) phase, so the closed-loop gain \(G/(1+T)\) is infinite
\(T(j\omega_x)=+1\)
\(T(j\omega_x)=0\)
\(|T(j\omega_x)|\) is very large with \(0^\circ\) phase
questions.explanation:
With \(T=-1\), the denominator \(1+T\) vanishes: a signal going around the loop comes back with the same size and inverted twice (the \(-180^\circ\) plus the subtraction), so it sustains itself without any input.
• \(T=+1\) gives \(1+T=2\), harmless in negative feedback.
• Large \(T\) at \(0^\circ\) is just strong, well-behaved negative feedback.

questions.prompt: At the frequency where \(|T|=1\), the loop-gain phase is \(-120^\circ\). What is the phase margin, in degrees?
questions.explanation: Phase margin \(=180^\circ+\angle T\) at the unity-loop-gain frequency \(=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ\). At least \(60^\circ\) is the usual target for a good design.

questions.prompt: A loop gain has \(T(jf)=\dfrac{1000}{(1+jf/1\ \mathrm{kHz})(1+jf/1\ \mathrm{MHz})}\). Find the frequency where \(|T|=1\) numerically and give the phase margin, in degrees.
questions.explanation:
The asymptotes say the crossover is near 1 MHz, right at the second pole, where the actual \(|T|\) is \(1/\sqrt2\) below the asymptote. Solving \(|T(jf)|=1\) gives \(f_c=786.2\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
\(\angle T(f_c)=-\tan^{-1}(f_c/1\ \mathrm{kHz})-\tan^{-1}(f_c/1\ \mathrm{MHz})=-128.1^\circ\), so PM \(=51.9^\circ\).
Using the asymptotic crossover (1 MHz) would give \(45^\circ\); the true answer is better because the crossover is lower.

questions.prompt: For the same loop gain (poles at 1 kHz and 1 MHz), what is \(\angle T\) at exactly 1 MHz, in degrees?
questions.explanation:
\(-\tan^{-1}(1000)-\tan^{-1}(1)=-89.94^\circ-45^\circ=-134.94^\circ\).
Two poles approach \(-180^\circ\) only asymptotically; at the second pole you are \(45^\circ\) short of it.

questions.prompt: In a loop with a dominant pole and one non-dominant pole, where should the non-dominant pole be placed for a comfortable phase margin?
options: Exactly at the unity-loop-gain frequency, giving \(90^\circ\) margin
Below the dominant pole
Anywhere: non-dominant poles do not affect stability
Well above the unity-loop-gain frequency, so it adds little phase where \(|T|=1\) (at the crossover it would give only about \(45^\circ\))
questions.explanation:
At crossover the dominant pole already contributes \(\approx-90^\circ\). A second pole AT the crossover adds \(-45^\circ\) (PM \(\approx45^\circ\)); at \(\sim1.7\times\) the crossover it adds \(\approx-30^\circ\) (PM \(\approx60^\circ\)). So non-dominant poles belong well above the crossover.
• A pole below the dominant one would make IT the dominant pole.

questions.prompt: A loop has \(L(s)=\dfrac{12}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}\). Its phase reaches \(-180^\circ\) at \(\omega=\sqrt{11}\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). What is the gain margin, in dB?
questions.explanation:
At \(\omega^2=11\): \(|(j\omega+1)(j\omega+2)(j\omega+3)|=\sqrt{12\cdot15\cdot20}=60\), so \(|L|=12/60=0.2\). The gain margin is \(1/0.2=5\), or \(20\log_{10}5=14.0\ \mathrm{dB}\): the loop gain could grow fivefold before the loop reaches \(-1\) and oscillates.
• \(-14\ \mathrm{dB}\) is \(|L|\) itself in dB, which has the opposite sign.
• 5 is the margin as a plain ratio, not in dB.
• \(10\log_{10}5=7\ \mathrm{dB}\) uses the power formula for an amplitude ratio.
questions.figure_alt: Nyquist curve of L: it starts at 2 on the positive real axis, swings clockwise through the lower half plane, and crosses the negative real axis at -0.2, well to the right of the -1 point.

questions.prompt: On a loop's Bode plot, \(|L|\) crosses 0 dB at 8 rad/s, where \(\angle L=-150^\circ\). The phase reaches \(-180^\circ\) at 20 rad/s, where \(|L|=-6\ \mathrm{dB}\). What are the phase and gain margins?
options: Phase margin 150°, gain margin −6 dB
Phase margin 30°, gain margin 6 dB
Phase margin 30°, gain margin −6 dB
Phase margin 60°, gain margin 6 dB
questions.explanation:
Phase margin is \(180^\circ+\angle L\) at the gain crossover: \(180-150=30^\circ\). Gain margin is how far \(|L|\) is below 0 dB at the phase crossover: \(0-(-6)=+6\ \mathrm{dB}\) (a factor of 2). Both are positive, so the loop is stable, though 30° is a thin margin.
• 150° is the phase lag itself, not its distance from \(-180^\circ\).
• A negative gain margin would mean \(|L|>1\) at \(-180^\circ\), an unstable loop.
• 60° doubles the phase margin.

questions.prompt: At the frequency where \(\angle T=-180^\circ\), a loop has \(|T|=0.3\). Is it stable?
options: No: any loop that reaches \(-180^\circ\) oscillates
Yes: the feedback is positive at that frequency, but with \(|T|<1\) the signal shrinks each trip around the loop (gain margin about 10.5 dB)
No: \(|T|=0.3\) is too small for feedback to work
It can't be determined without the DC gain
questions.explanation:
Oscillation needs \(T=-1\). With \(T=-0.3\), the closed-loop gain is \(G/(1-0.3)=1.43G\): a mild peak, not instability. The distance \(20\log(1/0.3)=10.5\ \mathrm{dB}\) is the gain margin.
Gotcha: reaching \(-180^\circ\) is not by itself fatal; it's the magnitude there that matters.

questions.prompt: Preview of margins in control design. A loop has \(L(s)=\dfrac{10}{s(s+2)}\), gain crossover \(\omega_c=2.86\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and phase margin 34.9°. A pure time delay \(e^{-s\tau}\) adds phase lag \(\omega\tau\) without changing \(|L|\). What is the largest delay the loop tolerates before it loses stability, in seconds?
questions.explanation:
Delay margin \(=\) phase margin in radians divided by the crossover frequency: \(34.9^\circ=0.610\ \mathrm{rad}\), and \(0.610/2.86=0.213\ \mathrm{s}\). A delay larger than this spends all the phase margin at crossover.
• \(34.9/2.86=12.2\) mixes degrees with rad/s.
• Multiplying by \(\omega_c\) instead of dividing gives 1.74.
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude of 10/(s(s+2)): falling 20 dB per decade, then 40 dB per decade, crossing 0 dB near 2.9 rad/s.

questions.prompt: Preview of robust stability. Besides gain and phase margins, a loop's 'stability margin' \(s_m\) is often quoted. On the Nyquist plot of \(L(j\omega)\), what is it?
options: The distance from the origin to the curve at gain crossover
The phase margin converted to radians
The shortest distance from the curve to the critical point \(-1\), equal to \(1/\max|S(j\omega)|\) with \(S=1/(1+L)\)
The value of \(|L|\) at \(\omega=0\)
questions.explanation:
Gain margin measures distance to \(-1\) only along the real axis, and phase margin only along the unit circle. The curve could still pass close to \(-1\) somewhere else. The minimum of \(|1+L(j\omega)|\) catches that, and its inverse is the peak sensitivity \(M_s\). Robust-stability tests build on this distance.
• The distance from the origin at crossover is always 1.
• Phase margin is one specific direction only.
• DC gain says nothing about how close the curve gets to \(-1\).
questions.figure_alt: Nyquist curve of a stable loop with the critical point -1 marked; the closest approach of the curve to -1 defines the stability margin.

questions.prompt: Preview of margins in control design. A widely used rule of thumb links phase margin to closed-loop damping: \(\zeta\approx\mathrm{PM}/100^\circ\) for PM up to about 60°. A loop designed with PM = 30° will have a step response that…
options: has no overshoot at all
oscillates forever
is slower than an over-damped design but never overshoots
rings noticeably, with roughly 35–40% overshoot (\(\zeta\approx0.3\))
questions.explanation:
\(\zeta\approx0.3\) gives \(M_p=e^{-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\approx37\%\). That is why designs usually target 45–60° of phase margin, which means \(\zeta\) of about 0.45–0.6 and modest overshoot.
• No overshoot needs \(\zeta\ge1\), far more margin.
• Sustained oscillation means zero phase margin.
• Low margin gives a fast, ringing response, not a slow one.
